chunks: From him, from Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from Ibn Muskhan, from Qutaiba, who said:

A man asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) while I was with him, saying: 'Sheep are sent out, and among them is the Jew and the Christian. If an illness strikes them and they are slaughtered, do we eat their slaughtered meat?' He said to him: 'Do not include its price in your wealth, and do not eat it, for it is merely the name, and one cannot be certain of it except from a Muslim.'
The man said to him: 'God has made the good things permissible for you, and the food of those who were given the Book is permissible for you, and their food is permissible for you.'
He said: 'My father used to say: It is only for small livestock and similar things.'

key_terms.طَعَامُ الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الْكِتَابَ: Food of those given the Book

ai.seo_question: What is the Shia ruling on eating meat slaughtered by Jews and Christians according to this hadith?
ai.summary: In this hadith from al-Isfahani's al-Isfār, Imam al-Sadi‘ (AS) addresses the permissibility of consuming meat from slaughtered animals belonging to Jews and Christians. While the questioner cites the general Quranic permission for 'food of the People of the Book,' the Imam clarifies that this applies specifically to 'habib' (small livestock like sheep) and similar animals, implying a nuanced view on the reliability of their slaughter practices. This reflects the Shia scholarly tradition of distinguishing between the textual permission and the practical certainty required for consumption, often favoring caution unless the slaughterer is known to be Muslim or their practice is verified.
